Individuals aged 65 years or older, as well as younger individuals, including children, who have high-risk conditions and are hospitalized between September and March, should be offered and strongly encouraged to receive the influenza vaccine prior to their discharge from the hospital. 2. Household members and others who will have contact with these individuals should be provided with written information explaining the importance of influenza vaccination and where they can obtain it. 3. Outpatient facilities that provide ongoing care to high-risk patients, such as hemodialysis centers, hospital specialty-care clinics, and outpatient rehabilitation programs, should offer the influenza vaccine to all patients during a single period shortly before the start of the influenza season. 4. Patients admitted to these programs during the winter months, after the initial vaccination program has been conducted, should be vaccinated at the time of their admission. 5. Household members of high-risk individuals should receive written information about the necessity of vaccination and where to obtain the influenza vaccine. 6. 7. Caregivers and other household members, including children, should be referred for vaccination to protect high-risk individuals. 8. Facilities serving individuals aged 65 years or older, such as retirement communities and recreation centers, should offer on-site vaccination to all unvaccinated residents or attendees before the influenza season. Alternatively, educational and publicity programs should emphasize the importance of vaccination and provide specific details on how, where, and when to obtain it. 9. Clinics and other healthcare providers for travelers should review indications for influenza vaccination before travel and offer the vaccine if appropriate. 10. Administrators of all healthcare facilities should arrange for influenza vaccines to be offered to all personnel before the influenza season begins. 11. Healthcare personnel should be provided with appropriate educational materials and strongly encouraged to receive the vaccine, with particular emphasis on vaccinating those who care for high-risk individuals, such as staff in intensive care units (including neonatal ICUs), medical/surgical units, and employees of nursing homes and chronic-care facilities. 12. Strategies such as using mobile carts to deliver vaccines to hospital wards or work sites and making vaccines available during night and weekend shifts may improve compliance. Follow-up campaigns may also be necessary if a community outbreak occurs. 13. The antiviral agents amantadine hydrochloride and rimantadine hydrochloride are specifically active against influenza A viruses. However, only amantadine is licensed for use in the United States. 14. These drugs interfere with the replication cycle of type A influenza viruses, though their exact mechanisms of action are not fully understood. 15. When administered prophylactically to healthy young adults or children before and during an epidemic, amantadine is approximately 70%-90% effective in preventing illnesses caused by naturally occurring strains of type A influenza viruses. 16. When given to otherwise healthy young adults and children for symptomatic treatment within 48 hours of influenza illness onset, amantadine has been shown to reduce the duration of fever and other systemic symptoms, potentially allowing a quicker return to normal daily activities. 17. Antiviral agents taken prophylactically may prevent illness but not subclinical infection, meaning some individuals may still develop immune responses that protect them against related viruses in subsequent years. 18. Side effects of amantadine may occur in a small proportion of individuals. While these symptoms are rarely severe, they may be significant for certain patient groups. 19. During influenza A outbreaks in institutions housing high-risk individuals, chemoprophylaxis should be initiated as early as possible to reduce the spread of infection. 20. 21. When used for outbreak control, amantadine should be administered to all residents of the affected institution, regardless of whether they received the influenza vaccine the previous fall. 22. The dosage for each resident should be determined after consulting the dosage recommendations and precautions outlined in this document and the manufacturer's package insert. 23. To minimize virus spread and disruption of patient care, chemoprophylaxis should also be offered to unvaccinated staff who provide care to high-risk individuals. 24. For prophylaxis to be fully effective, the antiviral drug must be taken daily for the duration of influenza activity in the community. 25. High-risk individuals vaccinated after influenza A activity has begun in the community can still benefit from vaccination. However, since antibody development in adults typically takes two weeks, amantadine should be administered during this period. 26. Children receiving the influenza vaccine for the first time may require up to six weeks of prophylaxis or until two weeks after the second vaccine dose has been administered. 27. Amantadine does not interfere with the antibody response to the vaccine. 28. Chemoprophylaxis should be considered for unvaccinated individuals who frequently interact with high-risk individuals in home settings, such as household members, visiting nurses, and volunteer workers, as well as unvaccinated employees of hospitals, clinics, and chronic-care facilities. 29. For employees unable to be vaccinated, chemoprophylaxis should continue for the entire period influenza A virus is circulating in the community. For those vaccinated during an active influenza A outbreak, chemoprophylaxis should be administered for two weeks after vaccination. 30. Prophylaxis should be considered for all employees, regardless of vaccination status, if the outbreak is caused by a variant strain of influenza A not covered by the vaccine. 31. Chemoprophylaxis may be indicated for high-risk individuals expected to have a poor antibody response to the influenza vaccine, such as those with advanced HIV infection. These patients should be closely monitored if amantadine is administered. 32. Chemoprophylaxis throughout the influenza season may be appropriate for high-risk individuals for whom the influenza vaccine is contraindicated due to anaphylactic hypersensitivity to egg protein or other vaccine components. 33. Amantadine can also be administered prophylactically to anyone wishing to avoid influenza A illness, with the decision made on an individual basis between the physician and patient.
